Sri Lanka’s Chemicals Industry Faces Severe Credit Freeze Amid Mounting Debt Concerns

Sri Lanka’s chemicals industry is grappling with a deepening financial crisis as a widespread credit freeze tightens its grip on manufacturers and distributors across the sector. The crisis, which began earlier this month, has seen banks and non-bank lenders sharply curtail credit lines to chemicals firms following concerns over mounting industry-wide debt and rising payment defaults.

Industry insiders say the situation has rapidly escalated, leaving many companies unable to finance imports of raw materials or meet payroll obligations. “The entire supply chain is coming to a standstill,” said Sarath Gunasekera, president of the Sri Lanka Chemicals Producers’ Association. “Without access to credit, even the most established firms are finding it impossible to maintain operations.”

According to data from the association, outstanding debt within the sector has surged by 40% over the past year, reaching an estimated LKR 82 billion by April. Several medium-sized firms, including Kelani Organics and Lanka PetroChem, have already suspended production, while others are reportedly operating at less than half of capacity.

“The banks are just not lending, even to long-standing clients,” said Ruwan Perera, chief financial officer of Southern Chemicals Ltd. “We have shipments stuck at port because we can’t pay our suppliers. If this continues, layoffs will be unavoidable.”

The crisis has sparked urgent calls for government intervention. “This sector is a backbone for agriculture, healthcare and manufacturing,” warned Manjula Dias, a union leader representing chemical plant workers in the Western Province. “If the freeze is not resolved soon, thousands of jobs could be at risk.”

As of today, there has been no official announcement of government measures to address the credit freeze. Industry analysts caution that without swift action, the chemicals sector could see a wave of bankruptcies before the end of the quarter.
